start_intro: You are the reactor operator. Keep the plant inside its envelope, follow grid demand and master the faults.
opt_cold_start: Cold start (reactor off, bring it up yourself) -- free play only
reactor_pwr_desc: Two separate loops, 158 bar, no boiling in the core. Power is set with control rods and boric acid. Every feedback is negative — forgiving, but slow to respond.
reactor_bwr_desc: A single loop, steam goes straight to the turbine. Recirculation flow moves power within seconds. At low flow and high power the density-wave instability is waiting.
reactor_rbmk_desc: Graphite moderated, pressure tubes, no full-pressure containment. At low power the void coefficient turns positive. The operating reactivity margin ORM is not a statistic, it is your life insurance.
alarm_help_none: No further explanation on file — the entry already speaks for itself.
stats_cfg_hint: Choose which values appear in the header bar -- separately per reactor type, saved for you. Applies immediately.
glossary_intro: The key terms in short — not a course, just a reference.
shortcuts_intro: Work anywhere during a running game, except while typing in a text field.
sc_escape_d: Close the active help window (alarm help, panel window, briefing)
gl_reactivity_d: How far the core sits from a self-sustaining steady chain reaction. Positive means power is rising on its own. pcm (hundred-thousandths) is the physical unit; $ (dollars) measures the same value relative to the delayed-neutron fraction — at 1 $ the chain reaction goes "prompt critical" (see there).
gl_period_d: Time for power to change by a factor of e (≈2.72). Short and positive means trouble is close. Infinite means stable.
gl_prompt_d: Reactivity reaches the delayed-neutron fraction (β, usually 1 $). From here the chain reaction sustains itself on prompt neutrons alone — power no longer rises over seconds, but over milliseconds.
gl_dnbr_d: Margin to the boiling crisis: how much power is left before the coolant film on the fuel cladding dries out completely and cooling breaks down. DNBR on the pressurized-water design, CPR on the two boiling ones — below 1 the limit is crossed.
gl_subcooling_d: Margin of coolant temperature below the saturation temperature at the current pressure. As it falls toward zero, the coolant starts boiling where the design never intended it to.
gl_xenon_d: Xe-135 builds up during operation and absorbs neutrons. After a power cut it keeps building for hours, fed by the decay of its precursor iodine-135 — reactivity keeps falling before it recovers.
gl_samarium_d: Sm-149 acts like xenon but is stable — it doesn't decay away, it has to be burned out by fissioning. After a long shutdown the poisoning just sits there instead of fading.
gl_orm_d: On the RBMK: how many control rods, in rod-equivalents, are still in the core. Not just a readout — it's the parameter that sets the void coefficient. The emptier the core, the more positive its response to boiling.
gl_void_d: How reactivity responds to steam voids in the coolant. Negative (pressurized- and boiling-water designs) is self-limiting: more steam means less reactivity. Positive (RBMK at low operating margin) is self-reinforcing.
gl_doppler_d: As fuel temperature rises, the U-238 resonances broaden and absorb more neutrons — always negative, acts instantly, and the fastest built-in brake on all three plant types.
gl_decay_d: Heat from the radioactive decay of fission products, which keeps going even after a scram — starting around 7% of rated power, then fading slowly over hours and days. The reason a shut-down core still needs cooling.
gl_scram_d: Reactor trip: every rod drives in at maximum speed. Named differently by control room — RESA in German, SCRAM in American usage, AZ-5 on the RBMK. Never fires on its own — what a given alarm means is in its own help text on the annunciator.
gl_annun_d: New (fast blink + horn): just came in, unacknowledged. Acknowledged (steady light): seen, cause still present. Cleared (slow blink): cause gone, but not yet acknowledged. Dark: everything normal.
empty_stage: This area is filled in a later version.
fault_body: The simulation reached an invalid state and was stopped. That is a bug in the game, not your mistake.
footer_note: Physically modelled, but a game — not a training simulator.
reactor_soon_hint: This type arrives in a later version. The pressurised water reactor is already playable.
ctl_boron_hint: Takes about three minutes to arrive.
trip_power_high_help:
Neutron flux above the trip limit (112% on the PWR/RBMK, 118% on the BWR) — the chain reaction is sustaining itself; without action, power keeps climbing within seconds.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor (SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5) immediately — nothing else acts fast enough.
• Find the cause before restarting: usually pulling the "Rods" too fast, or too big a step on "Demand".
• After resetting (annunciator), ramp back up slowly, in small steps.
trip_period_short_help:
Reactor period under 10 seconds with the chain reaction running — power doubles every few seconds, faster than any controller can follow.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor (SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5) immediately.
• Usually caused by pulling the "Rods" too fast, or an uncontrolled reactivity addition (e.g. boron dilution).
• Afterwards move rods much more slowly, or leave "Rod control"/the "Power controller" on automatic.
trip_pzr_press_low_help:
Pressurizer pressure below 132 bar — usually a leak (e.g. a stuck relief valve) or too much spray with too little heat.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor — the margin to the boiling crisis (DNBR) falls with pressure.
• Check "Pressuriser heaters": if on automatic and not enough, add heat by hand briefly.
• Back off "Pressuriser spray" if it's open by hand.
• If pressure keeps falling, check the "PORV open" alarm — the valve may be stuck.
trip_pzr_press_high_help:
Pressurizer pressure above 166 bar — usually too little spray during a power rise, rarer a stuck relief valve.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor.
• Open "Pressuriser spray" by hand if automatic isn't keeping up.
• Back off "Pressuriser heaters".
• Ramp power more slowly afterwards — fast rises are the usual cause.
trip_pzr_level_low_help:
Pressurizer level below 17% — not a trip condition yet, but the step before the pressure falls.

Do this now:
• Check boron/feedwater injection — usually an unintended dilution or a leak.
• Slow the power rise until level recovers.
• If it doesn't come back, prepare for a real pressure excursion (see "Pressure low").
trip_dnbr_low_help:
DNBR below 1.3 — the margin to the boiling crisis at the cladding is nearly gone. Below 1.0 the water film breaks down and the cladding overheats locally within seconds.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor — DNBR won't recover on its own at this power and flow.
• Cause: power too high for the available coolant flow. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" — is every one running?
• After resetting, ramp up slowly and only add power once all pumps are running.
trip_sg_level_low_help:
Steam generator level below 25% — the tube bundle risks running dry, plus cavitation risk to the feedwater pumps.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor, or the steam generator loses its cooling effect on the primary loop.
• Check "Feedwater": if on automatic but level keeps falling, raise it by hand.
• Usually caused by a feedwater loss or too much steam demand (turbine/governor valve too far open).
alarm_sg_level_high_help:
Steam generator level above 78% — risk of water carrying over into the steam line and turbine (water hammer).

Do this now:
• Throttle back "Feedwater", switch to manual briefly and lower it if needed.
• Check whether a load step made automatic overshoot briefly — then waiting it out is enough.
alarm_sg_press_high_help:
Steam pressure in the steam generator above 84 bar — the governor valve isn't taking enough steam, usually because power is rising faster than the turbine follows.

Do this now:
• Check "Governor valve": if on automatic, open it further by hand briefly.
• Alternatively pull power back until pressure stabilizes.
• If pressure stays high, the "Steam dump" bleeds the excess straight to the condenser.
trip_rcp_lost_help:
Coolant flow below 60% of rated — at least one reactor coolant pump has failed or been shut down, the rest can't cool alone.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor.
• Check the "Reactor coolant pumps" row, click the failed pump to restart it if possible.
• Only add power again after resetting and with every pump running.
alarm_subcool_low_help:
Subcooling margin in the primary loop small — the coolant is approaching saturation, DNBR falls with it.

Do this now:
• Raise pressure ("Pressuriser heaters") or lower power before the DNBR limit is crossed.
• Check "Reactor coolant pumps" — lower flow makes it worse.
alarm_porv_open_help:
Pressurizer relief valve open — bleeds off pressure; sustained, it means coolant loss (a small leak).

Do this now:
• Fix the cause: usually pressure too high from too little spray or too much heat — check "Pressuriser spray"/"heaters".
• The valve reseats on its own once pressure falls below it — if it stays open, pressure and level keep falling (see "Pressure low").
alarm_turbine_trip_help:
Turbine tripped — no more load is being taken, all the steam now goes only through the steam dump and safety valves.

Do this now:
• Watch power and grid output, stabilize the plant.
• Find the cause, then reconnect via "Reconnect turbine" (grid panel) — the button only works once no reactor protection is standing.
trip_clad_temp_help:
Cladding temperature above 1204°C — the fuel cladding is at risk, the next step is core damage.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor immediately.
• Make sure coolant flow is available (reactor coolant pumps or recirculation, depending on type) — usually a flow loss is the real cause.
• After resetting, keep power well below the design limit until the plant has recovered.
event_h2_explosion: Hydrogen explosion in the reactor building
event_time_skip: Time skipped ahead until the xenon had decayed
end_destroyed_body: Fuel enthalpy exceeded 963 J/g. The fuel is dispersed, the plant is lost.
trip_dome_press_high_help:
Dome/drum pressure above the trip limit — the governor valve isn't taking enough steam.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor.
• Check "Governor valve" (automatic/manual), open it further by hand if needed.
• "Steam dump" bleeds the excess to the condenser in the meantime.
• Usually caused by too fast a power rise — ramp up more slowly afterwards.
trip_level_low_help:
Level below 25% — core coverage at risk, the direct path to exposed fuel.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor.
• Check "Feedwater": if automatic isn't enough, raise it by hand.
• Only add power again after resetting, once level is stable in the normal band.
alarm_level_high_help:
Level above 78% — risk of water carrying over into the steam system/turbine.

Do this now:
• Throttle back "Feedwater", by hand if needed.
• Check whether a load change made automatic overshoot briefly — then waiting it out is enough.
trip_oprm_help:
Power oscillation detected (OPRM limit exceeded) — the operating point sits in the forbidden corner of the power/flow map: high power, too little recirculation flow.

Do this now:
• Trip the reactor — the oscillation keeps growing on its own until cladding damage threatens.
• Cause: "Recirculation flow" was too low for the power being run.
• Next time raise flow first before chasing power with the rods, or pull power back in time.
alarm_instability_help:
Signs of a power oscillation (decay ratio near 1) — not an OPRM trip yet, but the step before it.

Do this now:
• Raise "Recirculation flow" — more flow damps the oscillation directly.
• Alternatively pull power back until the operating point leaves the forbidden corner of the map.
• Don't ignore both: without action the oscillation grows until OPRM trips.
alarm_recirc_low_help:
Recirculation flow low at high power — instability risk, see flow instability.

Do this now:
• Raise "Recirculation flow" before power climbs further.
• If that's not enough, pull power back instead of holding it up with the rods.
alarm_msiv_closed_help:
Main steam isolation valves closed — no steam to the turbine, reactor pressure rising because the heat has nowhere to go.

Do this now:
• Find the cause (a disturbance, or closed by mistake).
• Only once the cause is gone: set "Main steam isolation" to "open" — reopening before that won't help if the reason for closing is still there.
• Until then, watch dome pressure (see "Dome pressure high").
alarm_srv_open_help:
Safety/relief valve has lifted — bleeds off pressure, and steam or coolant is lost with it.

Do this now:
• Fix the cause (pressure too high) — usually "Governor valve" too tight or power too high for steam demand.
• The valve reseats on its own once pressure falls below it.
alarm_cont_press_high_help:
Containment pressure above 3.5 bar — the relief valve is blowing steam into the suppression pool with nowhere else for the containment itself to release it. Above 4.3 bar the containment risks failing outright.

Do this now:
• Open "Containment vent" before the design limit is reached — a controlled release beats an uncontrolled rupture.
• Then address the cause so the relief valve stops lifting (see "Dome pressure high").
• If hydrogen is building up at the same time, vent as early as possible — the longer you wait, the more accumulates.
alarm_h2_critical_help:
Hydrogen from the zirconium-water reaction inside containment — the cladding is already damaged, even though the core isn't "destroyed" by the enthalpy limit yet.

Do this now:
• Vent immediately, before more accumulates — hydrogen that finds its own way out late and in large volume can explode inside the reactor building (exactly what happened at Fukushima Unit 1 in 2011).
• Address the cause: lower cladding temperature wherever possible — check the isolation condenser/fire injection.
• This alarm doesn't reverse once the cladding is damaged — from here on the only thing that matters is not losing the core any further.
alarm_orm_low_help:
Operating reactivity margin (ORM) below 30 rod-equivalents — outside the permitted operating band by procedure, even though no trip has fired yet.

Do this now:
• Insert rods ("Rods" → Insert) instead of withdrawing further.
• Don't raise power further until ORM is back above 30.
• The lower the ORM, the more positive the void coefficient (see the Basics glossary).
alarm_orm_critical_help:
Operating reactivity margin below 15 — critical: a scram right now inserts POSITIVE reactivity for the first few seconds (graphite-tip effect) instead of shutting down.

Do this now:
• Insert rods immediately, while ORM still allows doing it by hand.
• Lower power.
• Pressing AZ-5 now is risky — only as a last resort (see the Basics glossary entry "SCRAM / RESA / AZ-5").
alarm_void_positive_help:
Void coefficient strongly positive (low operating margin) — more steam voids in the coolant now mean more reactivity, not less. The core reinforces itself.

Do this now:
• Make sure "Main circulation pumps" are running — enough flow keeps the void fraction in the core low.
• Avoid running in the low-power band, where the effect is strongest.
• Raise the operating margin (insert rods) — that directly tames the coefficient.
alarm_mcp_cavitation_help:
Trip condition: subcooling under 4K and flow over 90% of rated at the same time — the pumps are running too fast for water this hot and close to boiling.

Do this now:
• Lower the "Main circulation pumps" control — less flow reduces suction losses at the pump, easing cavitation directly.
• At the same time check drum pressure — should sit near 69 bar. Too low means saturation temperature falls, the water is closer to boiling, subcooling shrinks.
• Check drum level — too little feedwater lets hotter, more void-laden water flow back to the pumps instead of cool water.
alarm_graphite_hot_help:
Graphite temperature above 760°C — the moderator is overheating. With its long time constant (about 35 minutes) this reading responds late, and it also takes just as long to come back down.

Do this now:
• Lower power and hold it there — countermeasures only take effect after minutes, not instantly.
• Not a trip condition by itself, but a sign of running too much power for too long.
alarm_axial_tilt_help:
Axial power tilt above 35% — the top or bottom half of the core is carrying noticeably more power than the rest, usually a xenon oscillation rather than the rods themselves.

Do this now:
• Check "Rods" — both groups move together on the RBMK, a tilt usually comes from the xenon distribution.
• Don't raise power further until the profile evens out — depending on the xenon state that can take hours (see the Basics glossary entry "Xenon poisoning").
az5_hint: AZ-5 drives every rod in over 18 seconds — graphite tips first.
scn_free_desc: No orders, no score. The plant is yours.
scn_pwr_load_follow_brief: Day shift at the pressurized-water plant. At midday the grid pulls its load back — heavy industry easing off together — and your unit is to follow it down, then climb back up through the afternoon, staying inside the demand curve throughout. Normally the control rods handle load changes like this: small, barely noticeable moves. But somewhere in this shift a rod bank jams, likely a drive fault, and there's no time to fix it mid-run. From then on boron is the only lever left for reactivity — and boron is slow: a good three minutes before a concentration change even reaches the core. Fail to plan for that lag, and you fall behind the curve.
scn_pwr_turbine_trip_brief: Full-power shift at the pressurized-water plant — until, ten minutes in, the turbine trips without warning. The generator drops off the grid instantly, but the reactor keeps making the same heat it always did: it now has to go straight to the condenser through the steam dump system, while the pressurizer and steam generator level swing out of balance. Just as you get that under control, feedwater regulation fails too — from there you're chasing level by hand while pressure tries to settle. Two faults that would each be manageable alone, arriving back to back.
scn_bwr_flow_brief: Three hours of load following at the boiling-water plant, this time driven through recirculation flow rather than the rods — the usual method here for smaller, fast load changes. The grid wants less at midday and more again in the afternoon; you follow by steering throughput across the power/flow map. The excluded corner sits where high power meets low flow — the decay ratio of the power oscillation that forms there grows instead of dying out. Partway through, the recirculation pump runs back on its own, unrequested: flow drops, and that forbidden corner gets closer whether you asked for it or not.
scn_bwr_msiv_brief: Full power at the boiling-water plant, a quiet first few minutes — then, seven minutes in, the main steam isolation valves shut without warning. The steam path to the condenser is gone, pressure in the reactor vessel spikes, and as pressure climbs the voids in the core collapse. Fewer voids means more moderation, means positive reactivity — arriving exactly when there is the least time to spare. You have seconds, not minutes, to respond.
scn_rbmk_night_brief: Night shift on the RBMK, in the middle of a planned grid test: power is to come down from 1000 to 200 megawatts, hold there for a while, then climb back up — on paper, a routine exercise. But 200 megawatts is exactly where this reactor type turns dangerous. Xenon builds up and eats into reactivity, forcing the control rods further out to compensate — and that eats into the operating reactivity margin, the number of rod-equivalents that must stay available in the core for an emergency. Below 30 rods, operation is already against the rules. Below 15, the AZ-5 scram stops being a safety function and becomes its opposite: the graphite tips that insert first displace what little moderation is left where the water has already boiled away, igniting reactivity instead of killing it. The power regulator drops out mid-shift, and shortly after, two main circulation pumps trip — both have to be caught by hand while the shutdown margin keeps shrinking.
scn_pwr_porv_brief: A quiet full-power shift at the pressurized-water plant — until, sometime in the first quarter hour, the pressurizer relief valve opens as designed to bleed off a small pressure rise, and then sticks: it stays open, while the control board still reports it shut. Pressure and level in the pressurizer fall as coolant quietly bleeds away through the open valve. The annunciator warns early, if you're watching for it — trust the position indication over the alarm, and you lose subcooling margin first, then the margin to boiling at the fuel surface (DNBR). The exact failure that started the Three Mile Island accident in 1979 — there, because no one trusted the contradiction between the two readings.
scn_bwr_fukushima_brief: Five minutes into the shift, the earthquake: automatic scram and isolation, the isolation condenser takes over decay-heat removal exactly as designed — no power needed for its core function. Fifty minutes later, the tsunami: total loss of power, AC and DC both gone at once. The isolation condenser fails to its safe default position — SHUT — and stays there, unnoticed, because its own indicator needs the very power that just disappeared and keeps showing its last known state. From here on, only what needs no electricity at all still works — valves opened by hand, gravity, and the decay heat still sitting in the core with nowhere else to go.
scn_bwr_instab_brief: Full-power shift at the boiling-water plant, grid demand staying high — then the main recirculation pumps drop back to low flow on their own, nothing you asked for. Power doesn't follow immediately, tempting you to chase it with the control rods instead of restoring flow first. That's exactly what drives the core into the excluded corner of the power/flow map: high power, low flow. There, a density-wave oscillation grows by itself, with no further cause needed, until the OPRM power limiter trips — and the scram doesn't fire on its own; you have to trigger it yourself when it's time.
scn_rbmk_cold_brief: Early shift after a two-week outage: the unit stands completely cold, every control rod fully inserted, the main circulation pumps stopped. Your job: bring the plant from shutdown onto the grid. First start the circulation pumps and establish flow, then ease the rods out until the core goes critical and power starts to climb. On an RBMK, that climb is the most dangerous part of the shift: the fuel is still cold, so the Doppler effect — the strongest natural brake against rising power — is weak, and the positive void coefficient carries more weight than it would at full power. You have to pass through the same 200-megawatt zone the night shift warns about, only this time climbing up into it instead of sitting in it — starting with the shutdown margin nearly full, but every centimeter of rod withdrawn spends down the very margin you'd need in a real fault. Target: 900 megawatts, without ever letting that margin fall below 30 rod-equivalents — and without ever seeing 15.

btn_scram_resa_title: Reactor trip — all control rods insert
btn_scram_az5_title: Emergency protection, category 5 — all rods insert over 18 seconds, graphite tips first
login_rate_limited: Too many attempts. Please wait a minute.
login_expired: Your session expired. Please sign in again.
hint_gov: In manual you hold the valve position yourself — power follows.
hint_fw: In manual you fill or drain the steam generator yourself.
hint_pzr: Heating raises pressure, spray lowers it.
hint_rods: In manual you drive the rods with Withdraw and Insert.
hint_low_power: At very low power, thermal power barely tells you anything -- it stays at 0.0% long before anything is actually happening. Period and reactivity balance react much earlier and already show progress while you withdraw rods.
hint_annun: Click a tile to see what to do.
